analysis.one_liner: Requires power plants, incinerators, and industrial facilities to cut mercury emissions by 95 percent.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with support from three senators of both parties, never got a committee vote or hearing and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Air Act to force the biggest mercury emitters — coal-fired power plants, industrial boilers, solid waste and medical waste incinerators, chlor-alkali chemical plants, and Portland cement plants — to cut their mercury emissions by at least 95 percent from their own baselines. It also required labeling of mercury-containing products like batteries and fluorescent bulbs, annual public reporting of facility-by-facility emissions, and federal research and public warnings aimed at pregnant women and children, the groups most at risk from mercury. The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who live downwind of coal plants and eat fish from contaminated lakes and rivers. The bill's own findings note that pregnant women, their fetuses, women of childbearing age, children, and people who subsist on fish face the greatest mercury health risks, and that the number of state fish-consumption advisories rose from 899 in 1993 to 1,675 in 1996 [S3]. It would also have given the public annual facility-specific mercury emissions data [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Pregnant women, children, and people who eat fish

how_it_helps.text: Requires each covered power plant, industrial boiler, incinerator, chlor-alkali plant, and cement plant to cut annual mercury emissions by at least 95 percent below its own baseline [S2][S3].

Requires labeling of mercury-containing products such as batteries, fluorescent bulbs, thermostats, and switches, and requires solid waste incinerators to separate those items from the waste stream before burning [S2][S3].

Requires annual public reporting of facility-specific mercury emissions and directs the EPA to improve the consistency of state fish-consumption advisories, which in 1997 were issued by 39 states [S2][S3].

Requires that captured mercury be disposed of so its hazards are not transferred to water, soil, or another environmental medium, and funds long-term research on permanently stabilizing mercury waste [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal-fired electric utilities, industrial boiler operators, municipal and commercial waste incinerators, chlor-alkali chemical plants, and cement manufacturers, which would bear the cost of monitoring, permits, and 95 percent emission cuts — costs typically passed through to electricity customers and product prices. Battery and bulb makers would also bear labeling and take-back-related compliance costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal power plants and heavy industry

drawbacks.text: The 95 percent reduction mandate applies to every covered unit, regardless of what control technology could economically achieve in 1998; mercury-specific control for coal plants was still developing at the time, so compliance costs could have been large and would typically be passed to electricity ratepayers [S2][S3].

Compliance is measured against each unit's own baseline using fuel-consumption data and regional estimates of mercury fuel content where direct data are unavailable, which critics could argue invites measurement disputes and gaming [S3].

The bill leaves medical waste incinerators and hazardous waste combustors subject only to reporting on reductions already required under existing standards, rather than imposing new 95 percent cuts on them [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefit is large and well documented in the bill itself: mercury is a neurotoxin concentrated in fish, children and fetuses are most at risk, and state warnings about mercury-tainted fish had multiplied in the 1990s [S3]. The cost falls on a small set of polluting industries and, in part, on electricity and product prices — the usual tradeoff of pollution control. The bill included flexibility (allowing trading among units at a single site if the site-wide 95 percent reduction was met) to soften costs [S3]. The main design weakness is that a flat 95 percent mandate written by Congress, rather than technology-based standards set by EPA, could have forced very expensive retrofits at some units.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Leahy introduced the bill on April 2, 1998, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S1][S5].
Three senators — two Democrats and one Republican — cosponsored the bill [S4].
No further action was recorded: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-fired power plants, chlor-alkali plants, cement makers, and incinerator operators are better off because the bill never moved: they avoided binding 95 percent mercury reduction mandates, permit requirements, and annual public disclosure of their emissions. People who eat fish from mercury-contaminated waters got no federal relief from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal plants, chemical and cement makers

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship (two Democrats and one Republican cosponsoring), but with only four total supporters and no votes ever taken, the record shows no party split on the merits.

industries.note: The bill names fossil fuel power plants as the largest source of U.S. mercury emissions and would require them to cut mercury by at least 95 percent, obtain enforceable permits, and report emissions publicly. Utilities would bear retrofit costs typically passed to electricity customers, while the public gains reduced mercury deposition in lakes and fish.

industries.industry: Chlor-alkali chemical plants using mercury cells
industries.note: Mercury-cell plants would face a 95 percent cut in direct and fugitive mercury emissions plus permits and monitoring. The industry's interest in continuing the mercury-cell process runs against the public's interest in less mercury in the environment.

Cement plants would have to cut mercury dust emissions by 95 percent and obtain permits. Cement prices could rise modestly, but the plants' mercury dust is a direct public exposure pathway the bill targets.

Incinerators would have to submit and execute plans to pull mercury-containing items out of the waste stream before burning, plus monitoring and reporting requirements. Many are municipal, so some costs would fall on local taxpayers, in exchange for less mercury released when trash is burned.

Manufacturers of listed mercury-containing items would have to label them (or their packaging, for button cell batteries) so the items can be separated from trash. The compliance burden is small relative to the benefit of keeping mercury out of incinerators and landfills.
